title: Current, voltage and resistance
teaches: Current, voltage and resistance, measuring them with a multimeter, and Ohm's law in resistors and lamps

blocks.text: Every circuit in this workbook is live. Wires are coloured by their [[voltage|voltage]], from the deep blue of the battery's - end up to orange, and yellow dots move along them with the [[current|current]].[^conventional] Before you see the live circuit, you will often be asked to make a prediction, because testing your intuition against a working circuit teaches more than reading the answer.

Here is a battery and two identical bulbs in a line, one after the other. The current leaves the battery's + end, goes through bulb A, then bulb B, and back into the - end. The bulbs are covered up for now.

blocks.caption: A 9 V battery and two bulbs in series
blocks.task: Guess which bulb glows brighter, then lock it in

blocks.text: The current is the same everywhere in a single loop.[^ampere] Every bit of charge that leaves the + end returns to the - end, so the first bulb leaves the exact same current for the second. The bulbs take **energy** from the passing charge and turn it into light and heat.
If you change bulb B, bulb A changes at the exact same moment because the current all the way round is set by everything in the loop together.

blocks.title: Current in a single loop
points: In a single loop the [[current|current]] is the same at every point, while the parts transfer energy into light and heat.
Change any part of a loop and the current changes everywhere in it.

blocks.text: Copper is full of mobile electrons, about 85 billion billion billion (8.5 x 10^28) in every cubic metre, all of them there before you connect anything. A battery pushes on the charge that is already in the metal, setting the whole loop in motion at once.

blocks.caption: A lamp and a switch. The dots can move at the electrons' true pace.
blocks.task: Close the switch, then show the true pace

blocks.text: Two distinct speeds are at work here. The electrons themselves drift along at a fraction of a millimetre a second,[^drift] while the electric field that pushes them propagates at a large fraction of the speed of light, starting the whole loop moving together. A garden hose that is already full of water behaves the same way: turn the tap and water comes out of the far end right away, long before any drop from the tap has travelled the length of the hose.[^fields]

blocks.title: Electron drift and signal speed
points: The charge is already in the wire before the battery is connected, and the battery pushes all of it round the loop at once.
Individual electrons drift slowly, while the electric push and the energy it carries arrive almost instantly.

blocks.text: Current measures how much charge goes past each second, and [[voltage|voltage]] measures how hard that charge is pushed.[^volta] Voltage is always a difference in electrical potential between two points, so a single wire never has a voltage on its own. When a schematic says a point is at 5 V, it means 5 V above **ground**, the common reference point everyone has agreed to measure from. Here ground is the battery's - end, coloured deep blue.

A multimeter measures voltage with two probes. Put the red probe on one point and the black probe on the other, and the meter shows how much higher red is than black. Because a voltmeter has a very high internal resistance, practically no current diverts through it, and you can touch the probes to a working circuit without disturbing it.

blocks.caption: A battery, a resistor and a lamp, with a multimeter
blocks.task: Measure the voltage across the resistor

blocks.text: Follow the colours round. From the + end the wire is orange, all one colour, because a plain wire drops almost nothing. Across the resistor the colour slides down: that slide is the voltage across it. The lamp takes the rest, and the wire back to the battery is blue. Add up the drops round the loop and you get the battery's 9 V back.

Measuring current requires breaking the circuit. To count the charge going past, the meter has to sit *in* the loop so the current flows right through it: you open the circuit and connect the meter across the gap. In amps mode a meter has a very low internal resistance, acting almost like a plain wire, which lets the loop's current pass through unblocked but will short out any component you accidentally bridge across.

blocks.caption: The same circuit. Switch the meter to amps.
blocks.task: Put the meter in the loop and read the current

blocks.title: On a real bench
points: Most meters need the red lead moved to a separate socket, marked A or mA, to measure current. Move it back to the volts socket as soon as you finish, because touching an amps-mode meter across a battery creates a dead short.
If the meter reads nothing in amps mode, check its fuse. Blowing it is the most common way to find out where the probes go.

blocks.text: A [[resistor|resistance]] sets how much current a given voltage can push through it. For a resistor the current is proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance: **I = V / R**, with I in amps, V in volts and R in ohms.[^ohm] Doubling the voltage doubles the current. You can rearrange Ohm's law as **R = V / I** to choose a component: to let 9 V push 20 mA (0.02 A), you need 9 / 0.02 = 450 Ω.

blocks.caption: A 9 V battery and one resistor
blocks.task: Pick a resistor that lets 20 mA flow, within 5%

blocks.text: Nobody sells a 450 Ω resistor. Resistors are made in standard logarithmic steps, twelve to each power of ten in the common E12 series: 100, 120, 150, 180, 220, 270, 330, 390, 470, 560, 680, 820, then 1 kΩ and round again. When you see a 470 Ω resistor in a schematic, the designer probably calculated a value near 450 Ω and picked the closest standard part.[^e12]

Even then, Ohm's law describes the behaviour of specific materials at constant temperature rather than a universal rule of nature. A curve tracer makes this clear by sweeping the voltage across a part and plotting the resulting current at each step.

blocks.caption: A curve tracer: a supply you can turn, and a plot of the current it pushes
blocks.task: Trace the resistor, then guess and trace the lamp

blocks.text: The lamp's curve bends over as the voltage climbs. A cold tungsten filament has about a tenth of the resistance it has when glowing white-hot, and its resistance rises sharply as the current heats it up. That low cold resistance is why incandescent bulbs usually burn out the instant you flip the switch: for a few milliseconds the cold filament draws an inrush current up to ten times its normal operating current. Components with curved current-voltage plots are everywhere in electronics, including diodes, transistors and solar cells.

blocks.title: Meters, resistors and lamps
points: Voltage is measured across two points in parallel with the part, while current is measured through the loop by placing the meter in series.
For a resistor at constant temperature, I = V / R; calculate the resistance you need and pick the nearest standard E-series value.
Many components have non-linear curves instead of obeying Ohm's law; a tungsten lamp's resistance rises sharply as it heats.

items.question: Two identical bulbs are in series with a battery. How does the current through the second compare with the first?
items.why: In a single loop the current is the same everywhere, while the bulbs transfer energy out of the circuit as heat and light.

items.question: You close a switch on a long loop of wire with a lamp at the far end. When does the lamp light?
options: Once the first electrons from the battery reach it
items.why: The wire is already full of charge. The push travels at a large fraction of the speed of light, so every electron in the loop starts drifting together.

items.question: Where do the probes go to measure the voltage across a resistor?
options: One on each end of the resistor
In a gap cut in the loop
items.why: Voltage is a potential difference between two points, so you touch one probe to each end of the part without breaking the circuit.

items.question: Where does a meter go to measure the current in a loop?
options: In a break in the loop, so the current goes through it
items.why: In amps mode the meter has nearly zero resistance. Connected in series in the loop it measures the current; connected across a part it shorts that part out and usually blows the meter's fuse.

items.question: 9 V across 450 Ω pushes how much current?
items.why: I = V / R = 9 / 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA.

items.question: Compared with when it is lit, a lamp's filament at a low voltage has…
items.why: Cold tungsten has a much lower resistance than hot tungsten, so the lamp's current curve flattens out as the filament heats up.

learned: In a single loop the current is the same everywhere, and components transfer energy rather than using up current.
The wire is full of charge before the battery is connected; the push arrives almost at once.
Voltage is measured across two points, while current is measured through a break in the loop.
I = V / R for a resistor, and in practice you choose the nearest standard E-series value.
A tungsten lamp's resistance rises as it heats, giving it a curved current-voltage plot instead of a straight Ohm's-law line.

conventional.title: Conventional current
conventional.text: The dots move from + to -, the direction Benjamin Franklin assigned to electric flow in the 1740s before anyone knew what moved inside a metal. When J. J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897, physicists realized the mobile charges in a copper wire are negative and actually drift from - to +. Because positive charge flowing one way has the exact same electrical effect as negative charge flowing the other, every schematic symbol and datasheet still uses the + to - convention.

ampere.title: The ampere and the coulomb
ampere.text: Current is measured in amperes (A), named after the French physicist Andre-Marie Ampere, who worked out the forces between current-carrying wires in the 1820s. One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second, which works out to about 6.24 x 10^18 electrons per second.

drift.title: Drift speed
drift.text: The average drift speed of electrons in a wire is the current divided by the density of free electrons, the charge of one electron, and the wire's cross-sectional area: v = I / (n q A). For 1 A in a copper wire of 1 square millimetre cross-section, that speed is about 0.07 mm per second.

fields.title: Energy flow around the wires
fields.text: In the water-hose analogy, the moving water carries the energy inside the pipe. In an electric circuit, the drifting electrons set up electric and magnetic fields in the space around the wires, and those fields carry the energy from the battery into the lamp's filament. Lesson 4 returns to how power travels from source to load.

volta.title: Alessandro Volta's pile
volta.text: The volt is named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery in 1800 by stacking alternating discs of zinc and silver separated by brine-soaked cardboard. Before Volta's pile, researchers only had static electricity machines and Leyden jars, which discharged in a single brief spark rather than driving a steady current.

ohm.title: Georg Simon Ohm's experiments
ohm.text: Georg Simon Ohm published his law in 1827 after testing wires of different lengths using a thermocouple stack powered by boiling water and ice, because early chemical batteries dropped in voltage as soon as they delivered a heavy current. The unit of resistance, the ohm (Ω), was named in his honour.

e12.title: The E12 series
e12.text: Each E12 value is roughly 21% higher than the last (spaced by the twelfth root of 10), so any resistance you calculate falls within 10% of a standard part, matching the 10% tolerance of vintage carbon resistors. Finer tolerances use denser tables: the 5% E24 series has 24 values per decade, and the 1% E96 series has 96.
